newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian crops seen at mercy of El Nino.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian crops seen at mercy of El Nino.

text.p: Heavy rain is drenching Indonesia's South Sulawesi while South Sumatra is suffering from drought, threatening key export crops in both cases, industry officials and meteorologists said on Thursday.
Dry weather affecting much of the sprawling archipelago could spread because of the El Nino pattern forming off the South Pacific, they said.
"Some crops will be able to withstand the drought, but others will be hit," El Nino expert Istiklal Amin of the state Land and Agriclimate Research Centre told Reuters.
"Crops will feel the impact next year. And if next year is also dry, they will be hit twice (the following year)," he said, adding that oil palm and coconut output could be affected.

Global weather experts have warned about the fast and intense development of the El Nino system, sparking fears it could rival this century's worst such phenomenon, in 1982/83, which caused hurricanes, droughts, fires and flooding in 15 countries.
Produced by a disruption in the atmospheric system leading to changes in wind patterns and higher water temperatures in the Pacific, El Nino is expected to peak in December.
U.K. trade house E D & F Man said earlier this month that a drought between May this year and April 1998 in Indonesia and linked to the El Nino could affect Indonesian coffee output.
Independent U.K. consultant Landell Mills Commodities said last week that a strong El Nino could cut world cocoa production by between 200,000 and 300,000 tonnes.
Indonesia is the world's top coffee producer after Brazil and Colombia, and ranks third behind the Ivory Coast and Ghana in terms of global cocoa production.
Traders said coffee plants had begun to flower in the key growing region of Lampung in south Sumatra and that cherries had begun to form in highland areas.
"The flowering process is going on well, and cherries are already beginning to form up-country," one trader said. "But for nearly two months there has been no rain.
"For the flowering and fruiting to progress well, the trees will need rain," he said. "If the rains don't come over the next two months, there will be problems with production."
But traders said it was still too early to forecast output for 1998 as the harvest only takes place in April or May.
The Association of Indonesian Coffee Exporters has said 1997 output is expected to plunge by 160,000 tonnes to 290,000 tonnes from 1996 due to bad weather.
Ironically, traders in the key cocoa growing region of South Sulawesi said flowering and fruiting there was being threatened by too much rain.
"It has been raining heavily the past 10 days in key growing areas and I fear it might affect the flowering and fruiting taking place currently," one trader said.
If the rain continued, he said, the mid-crop, or smaller harvest, would be hit. The main harvest was expected to end at least a month earlier, in August.
Grain traders said the corn harvest in East Java was being closely monitored by players due to the possibility of output being hit.
"Many feedmills are taking precautionary steps by locking in imports in case the crop is affected," he added.
The East Java corn harvest is set to peak late in the year, but traders said crops arrivals so far have been relatively small.
